ety.text: Old French vapeurder. Old French vaporbor. Middle English vapour English vapor From Middle English vapour, from Anglo-Norman vapour, Old French vapor, from Latin vapor (“steam, heat”).

senses.d: Cloudy diffused matter such as mist, steam or fumes suspended in the air.
The gaseous state of a substance that is normally a solid or liquid.
Something insubstantial, fleeting, or transitory; unreal fancy; vain imagination; idle talk; boasting.
ex: For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
I am at this present very sick of my little vapour of fame.

senses.d: Any medicinal agent designed for administration in the form of inhaled vapour.
ex: The physician can now prescribe medicinal vapors to be dropped on some cotton placed inside the inhaler.

senses.d: Hypochondria; melancholy; the blues; hysteria, or other nervous disorder.
ex:
Jan 13, 1732, John Arbuthnot, letter to Jonathan Swift
He talks me into a fit of vapours twice or thrice a week.
"Shows you what a modern young woman can come to after all, doesn't it? Screaming, and collapsing with the vapours - Hell!"
The surcharge of the stomack from a gross vapour, and from the poise of some outward weight, are alike

senses.d: To become vapor; to be emitted or circulated as vapor.

ex: to vapor away a heated fluid
He'd […]laugh to see one throw his heart away, / Another, sighing, vapour forth his soul.
Running waters vapour not so much as standing waters.

senses.d: To use insubstantial language; to boast or bluster.
ex: […] an amusing character all but extinct now, but occasionally to be encountered […] vaporing in the groggeries along the tow-path.

senses.d: To give (someone) the vapors; to depress, to bore.
